strengths: Principled and rigorous mathematical foundation: The paper presents an elegant theoretical framework leveraging multiplicative invariant theory and Hironaka decomposition, proving that any planar group can be embedded into an affine reflection supergroup to construct continuous, symmetry-preserving representations without boundary seam artifacts.

Comprehensive coverage of the 17 planar groups: The submission completely derives and tabulates the explicit primary and secondary invariant bases for all 17 2D crystallographic groups (Appendix G), providing a self-contained, practical plug-and-play recipe for practitioners.

Diverse and impactful downstream applications: The utility of the symmetric representation is demonstrated across four distinct problems spanning visual pattern synthesis, manufacturable paper-cutting with connectivity constraints (including physical fabrication verification), text-guided topology optimization, and mechanical metamaterial design.

Zero-shot symmetry transfer with diffusion priors: Decoupling symmetry enforcement (built into the continuous representation) from generative priors and physical objectives enables zero-shot symmetry generation without requiring symmetry-specific training datasets or retrained diffusion models.

Clear presentation and thorough appendix: The writing is organized, figures are instructive, and the supplementary material provides extensive mathematical proofs (including an insightful analysis of why higher reflectional embedding holds for n <= 3 but fails for higher dimensions).
weaknesses: Approximate symmetry in pixel space for latent-space optimization: While the representation enforces strict symmetry in the latent space, decoding latents to RGB pixels via standard convolutional VAE decoders (and refinement denoising) can introduce slight pixel-level symmetry deviations due to edge padding and nonlinear decoder operations.

Optimization efficiency and SDS sensitivity: Relying on Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) per design requires several hundred gradient optimization steps and careful tuning of hyperparameter schedules (CFG, timestep annealing, volume weights), which can be computationally slow compared to direct one-shot feedforward generative workflows.

Limited evaluation scale: Quantitative comparisons on visual tasks rely on relatively small curated test sets (e.g., 17 prompts for pattern generation, 12 prompts for topology design) and aesthetic metrics (CLIP-A), where human evaluation or more extensive symmetry-error benchmarks would provide additional validation.

strengths: Principled and mathematically elegant formulation: The paper cleverly leverages multiplicative invariant theory and Hironaka decomposition to solve a fundamental issue in symmetric continuous representations—namely, that naive asymmetric-unit extensions introduce boundary seams for non-reflective planar groups. By embedding planar groups into affine reflection supergroups, the method guarantees seamless, continuous G-invariant representations.

Rigor and theoretical depth: The theoretical contributions are thoroughly grounded and proved (Theorems 3.2, 3.3, B.6, B.7, B.8, B.10, and C.12). The authors also provide a deep characterization of the dimensional limits (n=2, 3 vs. n>3) and an explicit, ready-to-use table of secondary invariants for all 17 planar groups.

Comprehensive, multi-domain applications: The proposed representation is validated across four diverse tasks spanning vision and mechanical engineering: symmetric pattern synthesis, paper-cutting design with a provable connectivity constraint (VTM), stylized topology optimization via numerical homogenization, and zero-shot metamaterial generation.

Strong empirical and physical validation: The work does not rely solely on perceptual or aesthetic metrics (e.g., CLIP-A); it includes physical fabrication of paper-cut crafts, rigorous comparisons with basis projection and MLLMs (under strict post-symmetrization fitting), and numerical FEA simulations for mechanical performance.
weaknesses: Reliance on SDS optimization: Like many Score Distillation Sampling pipelines, the downstream generation process involves per-instance optimization that requires careful scheduling of classifier-free guidance, timesteps, and learning rates, which can be computationally slow compared to single-pass forward generative models.

Scaling complexity for higher dimensions: Although the authors establish theoretical existence for space groups in 3D (n = 3), the group index r = [Wa : G] can be substantially larger than in the planar case (where r <= 4), which would require maintaining and evaluating considerably more coefficient fields simultaneously.

Evaluation metrics for pattern generation: While CLIP Aesthetic score is standard, it is known to have biases. The evaluation in Section 6.1 could be strengthened with human perceptual evaluation or user studies regarding visual fidelity and symmetry alignment.

strengths: Rigorous mathematical formulation: The paper resolves the boundary discontinuity problem of continuous symmetric fields by cleverly embedding planar groups into affine reflection supergroups and utilizing the Hironaka decomposition from multiplicative invariant theory.

Completeness of the construction: The authors provide explicit derivations, supergroup mappings, and secondary invariants for all 17 planar crystallographic groups (wallpaper groups), making the theoretical framework immediately actionable as a plug-in recipe.

Decoupling of representation and objectives: By enforcing exact symmetry directly at the continuous representation level, the framework achieves zero-shot symmetry control without requiring symmetry-labeled training data or group-specific model retraining.

Extensive and multifaceted evaluation: The method is validated across four diverse applications (text-guided pattern synthesis, paper-cutting design with physical fabrication, stylized topology optimization, and mechanical metamaterial design), demonstrating strong geometric fidelity and functional performance.
weaknesses: Optimization efficiency: Relying on Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) requires per-instance optimization spanning hundreds of iterations, which is computationally expensive compared to direct feed-forward conditional generation.

Approximate symmetry in decoded pixel space: In the visual pattern generation tasks, the symmetric continuous field is parameterized in the latent space of a pretrained VAE; because the convolutional decoder and subsequent refinement denoising are not strictly equivariant, exact pixel-level symmetry is only approximately preserved.

Sensitivity to optimization hyperparameters: SDS-based pipelines often exhibit sensitivity to initialization, learning rates, classifier-free guidance (CFG) schedules, and timestep annealing, which can affect reproducibility across diverse prompt domains.

Baseline comparisons for texture generation: The visual comparisons primarily contrast against general-purpose commercial MLLMs (e.g., GPT-5.2, Gemini) and post-hoc projection; further quantitative comparison against specialized periodic texture or symmetry-aware generative models would provide a more comprehensive benchmark.

strengths: Principled and elegant theoretical foundation: The authors rigorously formulate the problem of continuous symmetric representation via multiplicative invariant theory and Hironaka decomposition. Embedding planar groups into affine reflection groups to bypass boundary discontinuities is mathematically sound and thoroughly proved (including dimensional analysis for n=2, 3, and counterexamples for n > 3).

Complete and actionable constructive results: The manuscript does not stop at existence theorems; it explicitly derives and tabulates the affine reflection supergroups and secondary invariant bases for all 17 planar groups (Table 2, Appendix G), providing a concrete, plug-and-play recipe for practitioners.

Broad and versatile downstream applications: The method is validated across four distinct domains: text-to-pattern generation, paper-cutting design (incorporating connectivity via the Virtual Temperature Method and verified via physical fabrication), stylized topology optimization (balancing mechanical compliance/bulk modulus and text alignment), and zero-shot metamaterial design.

Clear separation of concerns: By baking exact group invariance directly into the continuous representation, task-specific losses (SDS, VTM connectivity, homogenization FEA) can be cleanly layered without requiring symmetry-specific training datasets or retraining generative diffusion models.
weaknesses: Potential symmetry leakage in latent-space decoding: For the visual pattern generation tasks, the symmetric continuous field is parameterized in the latent space of Stable Diffusion / SDXL. Although standard 2D convolutions are translation-equivariant, they are generally not equivariant to rotations or reflections. Furthermore, the post-optimization perturbation and denoising step prior to decoding is only noted to 'approximately preserve' symmetry. This introduces a subtle gap between exact symmetry at the latent representation level and exact symmetry in the decoded RGB pixel output.

Optimization efficiency of SDS: Relying on Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) requires per-instance test-time optimization taking hundreds of iterations (e.g., 200–800 steps with FEA or diffusion score calls), which incurs substantial computational latency compared to feed-forward generative models.

Baseline selection and perceptual evaluation: Comparing against prompting MLLMs (GPT-5.2 and Gemini 3 Pro) via post-symmetrization fitting is somewhat of a strawman, as general MLLMs are not architected for periodic or group-symmetric tiling. Comparisons against specialized periodic diffusion baselines (e.g., circular/roll padding diffusion or equivariant UNets) and human perceptual evaluations/user studies for visual aesthetics are missing.

Limited evaluation scale on downstream benchmarks: In topology design, the quantitative evaluation is conducted on a modest set of 12 stylization prompts from prior work, and paper cutting is demonstrated mainly on a handful of qualitative examples.

strengths: Rigorous and elegant theoretical foundation: The paper provides a deep, mathematically sound framework connecting crystallographic groups, algebraic invariant theory (Hironaka decomposition on Cohen-Macaulay rings), and continuous representation symmetrization. The theoretical analysis characterizing embeddings into affine reflection groups for n <= 3 and the counterexamples for n > 3 are novel and mathematically rigorous.

Decoupled, modular design: By encoding exact planar symmetry directly into the representation space via high-symmetry coefficients and secondary invariant bases, the framework cleanly separates symmetry enforcement from task objectives (diffusion priors, connectivity, homogenization). Table 2 provides an explicit, readily implementable recipe for all 17 planar wallpaper groups.

Comprehensive and diverse applications: The paper validates the framework across four disparate and challenging domains: text-to-pattern design across all 17 planar groups, manufacturable paper-cutting design (including physical cut-and-fold verification), stylized topology optimization, and zero-shot metamaterial design with diffusion priors.

Convincing experimental results: Experiments show that while state-of-the-art MLLMs fail to satisfy exact symmetries and suffer severe aesthetic degradation under post-symmetrization, the proposed method preserves both high aesthetic quality and exact group symmetries, while outperforming basis projection baselines in computational complexity and visual fidelity.
weaknesses: Computational overhead of SDS optimization: The generation pipeline relies on iterative Score Distillation Sampling (200–800 steps per sample) over a hash-grid continuous representation, which is considerably slower than direct single-pass or standard conditional diffusion sampling.

Exactness after refinement and latent decoding: In Section 5.1, the authors note that the latent representation is perturbed with moderate noise and denoised prior to convolutional decoding. While convolutional decoders and diffusion priors encourage symmetry preservation, post-processing outside the strict continuous field parameterization means the final output RGB image may only approximately satisfy the group symmetry. Clarifying the quantitative gap between latent symmetry and pixel symmetry would strengthen the claims.

Baseline comparisons: The comparison against text-to-image MLLMs (GPT-5.2 and Gemini 3 Pro) under zero-shot prompting is somewhat unsurprising given that standard foundational models lack explicit geometric group-invariance priors. Comparing against specialized periodic texture synthesis approaches or roll/circular padding extensions in latent diffusion would provide a more direct benchmark.

strengths: Principled and elegant mathematical framework: The paper provides a rigorous mathematical bridge between crystallographic group theory, multiplicative invariant theory, and continuous neural representations. Using Hironaka decomposition to decompose arbitrary planar group invariants into high-symmetry affine reflection coefficients and low-symmetry fixed bases is theoretically sound and solves the boundary seam/discontinuity problem of naive asymmetric cell extension.

Complete and constructive recipes: The authors thoroughly categorize all 17 planar groups and provide explicit algebraic formulas and supergroup pairings in Table 2 and Appendix D, making the methodology immediately practical and reproducible.

Comprehensive theoretical boundary analysis: The paper goes beyond 2D to characterize when this construction holds in higher dimensions (proving it holds for n <= 3 but fails for n > 3 due to the non-existence of higher reflectional supergroups), which provides valuable theoretical depth and insight.

Diverse and convincing applications: The method is validated across a rich variety of domains, including text-to-pattern design, physically cuttable paper-cutting with connectivity guarantees (via Virtual Temperature Method), stylized topology optimization with mechanical homogenization, and zero-shot mechanical metamaterial design.

Addresses a concrete failure mode in contemporary generative models: The experimental comparison effectively demonstrates that state-of-the-art vision-language models (e.g., GPT-5.2, Gemini 3 Pro) fail to preserve strict crystallographic symmetry, whereas the proposed representation guarantees structural symmetry without requiring symmetry-specific training datasets.
weaknesses: Approximate symmetry in image space vs. exact symmetry in latent space: While the continuous vector field in the latent space strictly obeys planar group invariance, Section 5.1 acknowledges that decoding via standard VAE convolutional decoders and diffusion denoising only approximately preserves symmetry due to architectural biases (e.g., boundary padding, receptive field effects). The distinction between exact latent-space symmetry and final pixel-space symmetry should be analyzed and measured more quantitatively.

Optimization overhead of Score Distillation Sampling (SDS): The generation process relies on per-instance SDS optimization (up to 800 steps per sample), which is computationally expensive and inherits standard SDS limitations (such as sensitivity to hyperparameters and guidance weights) compared to feed-forward conditional generation.

Relatively small quantitative benchmark for text-to-pattern: The evaluation on pattern design is conducted using a curated set of 17 prompts (one per planar group) evaluated with CLIP Aesthetic score. Expanding this to a larger, more diverse benchmark with user studies or quantitative symmetry metrics would further solidify the empirical claims.
